newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan stocks weathering manipulation probe.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan stocks weathering manipulation probe.

text.p: The detention of the host of a popular cable TV stock-tip show in a manipulation inquiry hit Taiwan speculative shares on Wednesday, but the wider market was unaffected in what analysts said was a sign of maturity.
Prosecutors on Tuesday night detained Tan Ching-lien, nicknamed Teacher Tan, on suspicion of violating securities trading laws, officials said.
Tan, an unlicenced stock analyst who allegedly used his big cable television audience to manipulate certain shares, was being held without bail and could not be reached for comment.
Prosecutors said Tan and his cable TV show had been fined in 1996 for stock manipulation but had continued to operate with little or no modifications of the show's format.

Taiwan's so-called speculative shares, those whose prices move sharply with little link to company performance, dropped sharply on word of Tan's detention -- with shares that "Teacher Tan" promoted on his TV show hit hardest.
One of Tan's favourites, car parts maker Jui Li Enterprise, plunged the daily seven percent limit to T$28.1 (US$1.02).
Brokers said the main weighted index suffered little or no impact from the case, edging 3.33 points higher to 7,149.54 on good showings by shares with solid fundamentals.
Officials and regulators praised the wider market reaction as healthy and rational, drawing a contrast to earlier years when such news might easily have triggered panic selling.
"From the market's reaction, we can see that investors have turned more rational now," watchdog Securities and Exchange Commission chief Lu Tung-ying told Reuters.
"From now on, our commission will work more closely with other related government offices to crack down on illegal stock manipulation to ensure the market's healthy development."
Finance Minister Paul Chiu said his ministry would not pressure the stock market in the new crackdown, saying judicial authorities were capable of an independent inquiry.
"The finance ministry will not particularly pressure the stock market," Chiu told journalists. "The event is now under the judicial authorities."
Chiu specifically welcomed Tan's overnight detention and said Taiwan investors should rely on qualified professionals.

"The crackdown on Teacher Tan will help the Taiwan stock market's long-term development," Chiu said. "We should let qualified, professional analysts do objective (stock market) analysis based on objective data."
Anaylsts said rising investment by institutional investors -- basing investment decisions mainly on fundamentals -- had helped make Taiwan's market more rational and resilient.
"With an increasing investment ratio...by institutional investors, the market is now more fundamentals-driven," said Nikko Securities research head Michael Hung.

Although Taiwan's market remains dominated by individuals, liberalising rules helped push holdings by institutions past the 10 percent level in 1996 to 10.7 percent of total market value compared to 8.1 percent in 1995, the watchdog commission said.

Of total 1996 holdings, 8.6 percent were with Taiwan institutions and 2.1 percent with foreign ones -- far below the 70-80 percent institutional investment levels in the U.S., Japanese and other mature stock markets.
